title: Honest bread
hook: Guru Nanak squeezes a poor carpenter's bread and it drips milk, a rich man's bread and it drips blood (Janamsakhi tradition)
carry: bread that drips milk, not blood

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyakama: no family line to give, so he gave the truth, and was taken in. Your line was the truth is enough. What plain truth did you tell? Day eighty-one.

Two invitations to dinner arrive on the same night. One is from the richest man in town: a big feast, the best food, everyone important will be there. The other is from a carpenter who lives down a side street, and dinner is a plain, rough flatbread made from a coarse grain. The choice looks easy. The guest of honor in today's story chose the other one. The guest is Guru Nanak, the first Guru of the Sikhs, and the story is about what's inside a loaf of bread. Today's story is honest bread.
screen: `TWO DINNER INVITATIONS.` → `THE RICH MAN'S FEAST.` → `THE CARPENTER'S ROUGH BREAD.`

segments.voice: Guru Nanak lived in Punjab, and Sikhs honor him as the founder of their path. Many stories about his life are kept in collections called the Janamsakhis, life stories told and written down by his followers. Sikhs treasure them as stories of the Guru, and they're separate from the scripture itself, the Guru Granth Sahib. Here's the story. On his travels, Guru Nanak comes to the town of Saidpur and stays with a poor carpenter named Bhai Lalo, eating the simple bread Lalo earns with his own hands. A wealthy official named Malik Bhago is holding a great feast, and he's offended that the famous holy man is staying in a carpenter's hut. He demands that Nanak come. When Nanak arrives, Bhago asks why he refused his fine food. So Nanak asks for two pieces of bread: one from Bhago's feast, and one from Lalo's kitchen. He holds one in each hand and squeezes. From Lalo's bread, the story says, drips milk. From Bhago's, drips blood. Bread made by honest work, and bread made by squeezing the poor. Whatever you make of the miracle, the point is plain. In Sikh teaching, kirat karni, earning an honest living, goes together with vand chhakna, sharing what you have, and naam japna, remembering God. A line in the Guru Granth Sahib says it simply: the one who earns by their own work and gives some away has found the path. And Lalo? His name even appears in one of Guru Nanak's hymns in the scripture. The feast is only in the story. The carpenter is in the hymn.
screen: `GURU NANAK AND THE JANAMSAKHIS.` · `LALO'S HUT, BHAGO'S FEAST.` · `MILK FROM ONE, BLOOD FROM THE OTHER.` · `EARN HONESTLY, SHARE, REMEMBER.` · then, large: `HONEST BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat something honestly made. If you have something to eat nearby, a piece of bread, some fruit, a cup of tea, hold it. If not, think of your last meal. Settle, and breathe. Think of the hands it passed through: someone planted it, picked it, carried it, baked it, stocked the shelf. Then think of your own hands, and the work that paid for it. Take a slow bite or sip if you can, and taste it properly. Let it be enough. The bell holds the time.
Honest bread. The carpenter's rough bread that, in the story, dripped milk in Guru Nanak's hand, because it was earned without harming anyone. Today's word.
Your line: bread that drips milk, not blood. Today, at one meal, think of the hands that made it, and share one small piece of what you have. Day eighty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago to teach kirat karni, honest work, alongside sharing and remembering God; the langar, the free kitchen at gurdwaras, shares food with anyone who comes.

fork.setup: you're Guru Nanak. the rich official demands to know why you ate a carpenter's rough bread instead of his feast. what do you do?
options: squeeze a piece of each bread
leave the town without a word
fork.reveal: he squeezes both. Lalo's bread drips milk, and Bhago's drips blood: bread earned honestly, and bread squeezed from the poor.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: kirat karni, earning an honest living by your own work, taught alongside sharing and remembering God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle about magic bread.
what it means: bread earned by honest work nourishes; bread squeezed from others carries their harm.
what a scholar hears: a Janamsakhi tale of Saidpur (Eminabad), linked to kirat karni and a hymn naming Lalo.

notes: Janamsakhi story paraphrased; versions differ in details (the bread grain, the feast as a brahm bhoj). Confirm the telling.
The line 'one who earns by their own work and gives some away has found the path' paraphrases Ang 1245: confirm Ang number.
Lalo named in Guru Nanak's hymn in Tilang (Ang 722–723): confirm.
Three pillars (kirat karni, vand chhakna, naam japna): standard Sikh teaching; confirm the order and Gurmukhi ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ.
Honorific: the script says 'Guru Nanak'; a Sikh scholar may prefer 'Guru Nanak Dev Ji' at first mention.
